title: Putting it into readable words
coreMove: Translate the already-earned structure into sentences that preserve its image instead of smoothing it into blur.
sourcePressure: Chapter 10 closes by putting structure into readable words: create the image first, then copy the image in words, keeping readability accountable to the structure it carries.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: Treating readability as pleasant phrasing, simplification, or style polish after the thinking is done.

sourceAnchors.name: create the image
sourceAnchors.detail: the Chapter 10 sidecar lists Create the image as an authorized heading before Copy the image in words
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: The sentence can only copy the image if the writer has first seen what the structure is doing.

sourceAnchors.name: copy the image in words
sourceAnchors.detail: the sidecar says readable expression is translation of structure rather than a substitute for it
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Readable words are successful when the reader receives the architecture without having to rebuild it silently.

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples, drawn from: timestamp+name+action, dialogue first line, sensory detail first, second-person direct address, retrospective recognition, question-as-hook, environmental detail before any human
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: C8 catches Cartesian repetition of phrases but not the deeper template of 'timestamp + named protagonist + prop + decision' that makes 6 examples feel like 1 example with name swaps

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one paragraph 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm through a direct second-person passage, a short research/source aside, a reader question, or a brief historical reference
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following the pattern 'concrete anchor sentence -> abstract rule sentence -> elaboration sentence'

exampleSpecs.domain: an urban-design studio led by Ada writing a public note about street changes
exampleSpecs.audience: planners turning structural reasoning into readable prose
exampleSpecs.stakes: residents will misunderstand tradeoffs if contrast and sequence blur into planning language
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Ada sketches the tradeoff first, then writes one sentence that keeps the before-after street image intact instead of hiding it behind improvement language.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Ada watches tracing paper curls over a crosswalk sketch and a bus-lane diagram.

exampleSpecs.domain: a materials scientist explaining a battery-test sequence to investors
exampleSpecs.audience: technical founders making complex sequence readable
exampleSpecs.stakes: investors will confuse cause and sequence if the sentence jumps from result to claim without the test path
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Jonas asks what image the sentence must carry, draws test, heat rise, failure threshold, and result, then writes the sequence in that order.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: What has to happen first for the battery result to make sense?

exampleSpecs.domain: a classical-music festival explaining ticket-tier changes
exampleSpecs.stakes: patrons will hear a price grab unless the sentence preserves the relationship between access and seat allocation
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Isabel replaces vague affordability language with a sentence that shows cheaper balcony seats are protected before premium orchestra prices rise.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: It took Isabel three angry draft replies to see the sentence had erased the structure.

exampleSpecs.domain: a cloud-infrastructure lead named Marco writing outage language for customers
exampleSpecs.audience: technical leaders translating cause and recovery clearly
exampleSpecs.stakes: customers will lose trust if the prose sounds smooth but hides the causal path of the outage
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: "Do not call it instability if the cause was a failed certificate renewal," Marco says, then rewrites the sentence to preserve cause, failure, and recovery order.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: "Do not call it instability," Marco says while the status page clock keeps counting.

exampleSpecs.domain: a community legal clinic writing an eviction-rights leaflet
exampleSpecs.audience: public legal educators making structure readable under stress
exampleSpecs.stakes: tenants may miss the action sequence if legal exceptions are smoothed into one dense paragraph
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: You watch Chiara draw notice, deadline, response, and hearing as four boxes, then write the leaflet sentence so the boxes stay in order.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: You are holding a draft leaflet beside four boxes drawn on a yellow legal pad.

exampleSpecs.domain: a specialty cycling shop explaining warranty exclusions
exampleSpecs.audience: retail owners writing customer policies without blurring categories
exampleSpecs.stakes: customers and staff will argue if crash damage, wear, and manufacturer defects are not linguistically separated
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: At 10:40 a.m., Ryan turns one pleasant warranty paragraph into three category sentences that preserve the structure customers need to compare.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: At 10:40 a.m., Ryan lays a cracked carbon rim beside the warranty card.
mustAvoid: bike helmet or generic shop-prop shells

skillTargets: preserve structural relationships in sentence wording
avoid smoothing contrast, sequence, or causality into vague prose
revise a sentence by copying the structure image more faithfully

tryThisNowSpec: Choose one sentence and write its relationship in the margin: sequence, contrast, cause, or category. Revise only to make that relationship visible.
